items.stem: In "The animal didn't cross the street because it was too tired", how does attention decide that "it" refers to "animal"?

options.text: The word "it" scores every other word on how well it matches what "it" is asking for, and animal scores highest.
options.feedback: The score is a similarity between positions. Tired asks for something that can be tired, and animal matches.

options.text: A grammar rule says a pronoun refers to the subject of the sentence.
options.feedback: No grammar rule is used. The result changes when the last word changes.
Street is nearer to "it" than animal is, and the model still picks animal.

options.text: It picks the noun that was read first.
options.feedback: Order of reading is not used. Every word is available at once.

items.stem: Before you try it: you change the last word from "tired" to "wide". What happens to what "it" looks at?

options.feedback: "It" builds its question from the words around it. Wide asks for something with width, and street matches.

options.text: It stays on "animal", because the nouns have not changed.
options.feedback: The question that "it" asks depends on the last word, so the weights change.

options.text: It spreads evenly across all words.
options.feedback: The weights stay concentrated on the best match.

options.text: It looks only at the last word.
options.feedback: The last word gets some weight, but the strongest weight goes to street.

items.try: Switch between the two sentences in the widget and compare the bars for "it".

items.stem: A prompt grows from 4,000 tokens to 8,000 tokens. Roughly how does the attention work change?

options.feedback: Every token is compared with every other token, so the work grows with the square of the length.
Doubling would be true if each token were compared with a fixed number of others. Here every token is compared with all the others.
The growth is quadratic: doubling the length multiplies the work by four.

items.stem: Why did attention remove the problem of the single note in recurrent networks?

options.text: Every word stays available, so any word can look directly at any other word, however far apart they are.
options.feedback: Nothing is summarized away. Word 1 and word 5,000 are one step apart.

options.text: The note was made much larger.
options.feedback: There is no note. The words themselves are kept.

options.text: The model skips most words and reads only the important ones.
options.feedback: All words are kept and compared.

options.text: Words are now read in a random order.
options.feedback: The order is still part of the input. The change is that reading order no longer limits what a word can look at.
